structured.recommendation: Adopt a progressive canary rollout with automated, metric-gated promotion and one-click/automatic rollback. This directly serves the stated goal of reducing deployment risk (issue:1) by exposing each release to a small traffic slice first and halting on regression, while preserving delivery speed (issue:2) because healthy changes auto-promote without manual gates. Concretely: deploy to 1-5% of traffic, watch error-rate/latency/saturation SLOs for a fixed bake window, then step to larger percentages; auto-rollback on SLO breach. This dominates all-at-once (fast but risky) and long manual staging (safe but slow), which is why it best answers issue:3. Prefer this over blue/green when you want graduated risk exposure and cheaper capacity; prefer blue/green if instant full cutover and rollback simplicity matter more than incremental exposure.

evidence.claim: Primary objective is reducing deployment risk
Hard constraint is preserving delivery speed, so a slow manual gate policy is disqualified
The decision requested is a single rollout policy that balances both objectives
Canary/progressive delivery with automated rollback is the standard pattern that trades a small bake window for large risk reduction without gating throughput

assumptions.statement: The deployment target can route a fractional slice of production traffic to a new version (load balancer, service mesh, or feature-flag capable).
assumptions.if_false_then: Canary is infeasible; fall back to blue/green or ring-based deployment instead.
assumptions.how_to_verify: Check the delivery platform (mesh/ingress/flag system) for percentage-based routing support.

assumptions.statement: There are real-time health signals (error rate, latency, saturation) reliable enough to gate promotion and trigger rollback.
assumptions.if_false_then: Automated gating cannot be trusted; add manual approval, which erodes the speed constraint.
assumptions.how_to_verify: Confirm metrics/alerting coverage and historical signal-to-noise on release regressions.

assumptions.statement: Releases are backward/forward compatible so old and new versions can serve concurrently during the canary.
assumptions.if_false_then: Concurrent-version serving breaks; require expand/contract schema migrations before canarying.
assumptions.how_to_verify: Review DB/schema and API contract change process for compatibility discipline.

risks: Issue is abstract: no data on service type, traffic volume, or current deployment method, so the recommended policy may not fit a low-traffic service where a canary slice is statistically meaningless.
Bad or lagging SLO signals can auto-promote a faulty release, giving false confidence.
Stateful/schema-changing releases can violate the backward-compatibility assumption and cause canary-specific failures.
Automation and mesh/flag tooling add operational complexity that itself carries risk.
what_would_change_my_view: Evidence that traffic volume is too low for a statistically meaningful canary would shift me toward blue/green or ring deployments.
A requirement for instantaneous full cutover with trivial rollback would favor blue/green.
Absence of trustworthy real-time SLO signals would push toward a defer_for_evidence position until observability exists.
Regulatory or stateful-migration constraints preventing concurrent versions would change the recommended mechanism.
structured.next_action: Confirm the two load-bearing capabilities — percentage-based traffic routing and trustworthy real-time SLO signals — then pilot an SLO-gated 5% canary with automatic rollback on one representative service.
